claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a thin native iron-oxide film.
The native iron-oxide film provides adequate corrosion protection to Q235 steel at room temperature.
The native iron-oxide film becomes unstable in molten salt at 700–900 °C.
Chloride ions flux the iron oxide and cause its dissolution and spallation.
Breakdown of the oxide exposes Q235 steel and accelerates its corrosion.
The native oxide on as-received Q235 steel is a thermally grown scale formed during processing.
Identical Q235 samples should be compared in room-temperature aqueous chloride and high-temperature molten salt.
The native oxide remains stable under ambient chloride exposure.
A sample with an enhanced protective coating can serve as a control for the native oxide.
Continuity, thickness, porosity, integrity, and adhesion of the native oxide determine its effectiveness as a corrosion barrier.
At room temperature, the oxide hinders further oxidation by acting as a diffusion barrier.
At high temperature, molten chloride attacks the oxide and causes film breakdown and accelerated substrate corrosion.
Room-temperature exposure will produce minimal mass change and a continuous, adherent oxide scale.
High-temperature molten-salt exposure will produce a discontinuous or cracked oxide layer.
High-temperature molten-salt exposure will cause significant mass loss in Q235 steel.
The proposed mechanism is limited to untreated Q235 steel and does not cover engineered protective films.
Salt composition and exposure time may alter the observed corrosion response.
Failure to observe increased mass loss or oxide-scale breakdown during high-temperature molten-salt exposure would falsify the proposed mechanism.
